historical_timeline.summary: Joined the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton.
Intermittent severe abdominal pain, worse toward the end of the year.
Exploratory laparotomy found an abdominal aortic aneurysm, which was wrapped in cellophane; discharged about three weeks later.
Gave a well-worn pipe to a friend; by then he had restricted his smoking on doctors' orders.
The aneurysm ruptured; he declined an operation.

claims.statement: Albert Einstein was born on March 14, 1879, in Ulm, in the Kingdom of Wurttemberg, German Empire.
Einstein died on April 18, 1955, at Princeton Hospital in Princeton, New Jersey, aged 76.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without detail.

claims.statement: He worked at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton from 1933 until his death and became a United States citizen in 1940.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Social context for the modern frame.

claims.statement: At about 69 he began to have intermittent episodes of severe abdominal pain, at times bad enough to make him vomit, which grew worse toward the end of 1948.

On December 31, 1948, at the Jewish Hospital of Brooklyn, the surgeon Rudolph Nissen performed an exploratory laparotomy and found an abdominal aortic aneurysm described as the size of a grapefruit; because it could not be removed with the surgery of the time, he wrapped its front in cellophane to provoke scarring that might prevent growth and rupture.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern aneurysm; the operation is past history, and the documented size is not used in the synthetic episode.

claims.statement: He recovered slowly and left the hospital about three weeks after the operation.

In April 1955 the abdominal pain returned, more severe; the aneurysm had enlarged and ruptured. A surgeon advised an urgent operation, but Einstein, admitted to Princeton Hospital, declined it, saying in substance that he had lived long and did not wish to prolong his life artificially. An autopsy confirmed a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History only; the modern episode records synthetic preferences and does not stage this.

claims.statement: Einstein was a long-time pipe smoker; a pipe was characteristic of his appearance, and an account of his aneurysm says he had smoked constantly since adolescence.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic nicotine dependence and the cessation plan.

claims.statement: In his later years he restricted his smoking on doctors' orders but kept holding a pipe; in 1953 he gave a pipe worn through at the bit to a friend.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Claim only, after the index date; the modern habit of holding an empty pipe after quitting is synthetic.

claims.statement: The picture of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm mimicking acute cholecystitis has been called the Einstein sign, after his final illness.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Teaching context for the emergency symptom plan; claim only.

claims.statement: Retrospective writers have suggested that he had features of the autism spectrum.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; not a modern diagnosis and not used in the episode.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: First six months of care of a 70-year-old man with an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm below the repair threshold, known since an exploratory laparotomy at which it was wrapped rather than repaired: baseline duplex ultrasound and CT angiography, surveillance every six months at 5.0 to 5.4 cm, blood pressure below 130/80, a high-intensity statin, low-dose aspirin for aortic atheroma, smoking cessation with nicotine replacement, avoidance of fluoroquinolones, education about symptoms that need emergency care, and a documented shared decision with vascular surgery about elective repair thresholds (5.5 cm in men, rapid growth, or symptoms) and endovascular versus open repair, following the Society for Vascular Surgery 1941 and ACC/AHA 1945 guidelines with the CMID hypertension and hyperlipidemia monographs. His preferences are recorded as synthetic shared decision-making; the decision he made at the end of his life is history only.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Einstein is a 70-year-old man with a 5.0 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm by duplex ultrasound, found and wrapped at a prior exploratory laparotomy, who returns four weeks after his first visit for the CT angiography results and is seen by vascular surgery on the same day. He has had no abdominal, back, or flank pain, fainting, or leg symptoms. He stopped smoking on his quit date a week after the first visit and has had no tobacco for three weeks. He wears the 14 mg patch daily and uses three or four lozenges a day, and he holds an empty, unlit pipe while he works, which he finds helps. He started losartan 50 mg and atorvastatin 40 mg four weeks ago without side effects; his home blood pressure readings average 134/80. The CT angiography two weeks ago showed a 5.2 cm fusiform infrarenal aneurysm with a 2.2 cm neck, calcified atheroma of the aorta and iliac arteries, thickening along the front of the aneurysm from the old wrapping, and no fluid around the aorta.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Einstein returns about four months after his first visit. He has had no tobacco since his quit date and has had no cravings strong enough to need more than one or two lozenges a day for the past month; he still holds an empty pipe at his desk. His home blood pressure readings average 124/74 on amlodipine 5 mg and losartan 100 mg. He takes atorvastatin 40 mg and aspirin 81 mg without muscle aches, bruising, or bleeding. The back strain six weeks ago settled within ten days, and he has had no abdominal, back, or flank pain since. The lipid panel was not drawn in the first twelve weeks on atorvastatin, because no standing order was placed after the four-week visit; it was drawn today.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Einstein is a 70-year-old man with a 5.0 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm under surveillance, who calls and is seen the same day because of low back pain. Two days ago he carried several boxes of books up a flight of stairs at his office and felt a pulling pain across the right lower back the next morning. The pain is a dull ache, 4 out of 10, worse when he bends, twists, or gets out of a chair, and eased by lying flat and by a heating pad. It does not spread to the abdomen, flank, groin, or legs. He has had no abdominal pain, fainting, lightheadedness, sweating, numbness, weakness, or change in bladder or bowel control, and no fever. He remembered the aneurysm card and called rather than waiting, as he was taught. He has taken acetaminophen 500 mg twice. He takes amlodipine, losartan 100 mg, atorvastatin, and aspirin, and has had no tobacco since his quit date.

referral.question: Infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm of 5.0 cm by duplex ultrasound in a 70-year-old man, found at an exploratory laparotomy for abdominal pain and wrapped rather than repaired. Please advise on surveillance, the thresholds and options for elective repair, and medical therapy, and record a shared decision with him
referral.urgency: Routine, within four weeks, on the same day as his CT angiography results visit
referral.pertinent_history: Episodes of severe abdominal pain led to an exploratory laparotomy, at which an abdominal aortic aneurysm was found; it could not be removed, and its front was wrapped to provoke scarring. He has had no abdominal pain since. Duplex ultrasound today: infrarenal aorta 5.0 cm. CT angiography ordered for anatomy. Pipe smoker since his youth, about five or six bowls a day; quit date set for next week with a 14 mg nicotine patch and 2 mg lozenges. Hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg, 146/86 mmHg today; losartan 50 mg added. Atorvastatin 40 mg started; LDL 142 mg/dL. Creatinine 1.02 mg/dL, eGFR 77, potassium 4.3, HbA1c 5.6 percent, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 14 mg/g, hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL, platelets 232. No diabetes, angina, stroke, or claudication. Independent, works most days, walks an hour a day. Weight 79 kg, BMI 26.7. No known allergy
questions: Does the CT angiography confirm an aneurysm below the repair threshold, and does the old wrapping change his risk or the plan?
How often, and by which test, should the aneurysm be measured?
At what diameter, growth rate, or symptoms would you advise elective repair, and is his anatomy suitable for endovascular repair?
What medical therapy do you advise: blood pressure target, statin, and antiplatelet therapy?
Should other arteries be checked for aneurysms?
Please record a shared decision with him about repair, including his preferences

consultant_note.history: Mr. Einstein, a 70-year-old theoretical physicist, is seen at the request of Dr. Ward for an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm. Episodes of severe abdominal pain led to an exploratory laparotomy, at which the aneurysm was found and its front wrapped rather than repaired; the pain has not returned. He has no back, flank, or groin pain, fainting, claudication, or cold or painful toes. He stopped his pipe three weeks ago and uses a nicotine patch and lozenges. He takes amlodipine, losartan, which was started four weeks ago, and atorvastatin. He walks an hour a day and has no chest pain or breathlessness on exertion. He asked for exact figures and for the reasoning behind each recommendation
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Ward's notes from the first visit; the duplex ultrasound report from four weeks ago (5.0 cm); the CT angiography images and report from two weeks ago; today's metabolic panel (potassium 4.6, creatinine 1.08 mg/dL, eGFR 72); baseline lipids, HbA1c, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, and blood count; today's 12-lead ECG (sinus rhythm at 70, normal intervals, no left ventricular hypertrophy or Q waves); and today's vital signs

exam.finding: Well; weight 78.6 kg
Regular rhythm at 70 per minute; blood pressure 136/82 mmHg in both arms; no carotid or abdominal bruits
Pulsatile, expansile, non-tender mass above the umbilicus; healed midline scar
Femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses normal and equal; no femoral or popliteal aneurysm felt; feet warm with normal capillary refill

assessment.assessment: Fusiform infrarenal aneurysm of 5.2 cm by CT outer-wall measurement and 5.0 cm by ultrasound, asymptomatic and below the 5.5 cm threshold for elective repair in men. The difference between the two tests is the usual one, so ultrasound should be used consistently to follow it. The wrapping produced the thickening seen along the front wall; it does not reliably prevent growth or rupture, and it does not change the thresholds or the surveillance interval. In trials of aneurysms below 5.5 cm, early repair did not improve survival over surveillance
At 5.0 to 5.4 cm in a man, duplex ultrasound every six months is recommended, with CT if the views are poor or repair is being planned

Elective repair is advised at 5.5 cm, at growth of 0.5 cm or more in six months, or with pain or tenderness attributable to the aneurysm. His anatomy suits endovascular repair: a neck 2.2 cm wide and 2.0 cm long with 30 degrees of angulation and iliac arteries of 1.3 cm. Open repair would be harder after the previous laparotomy and the scarring around the wrapped aorta. Endovascular repair carries a lower early risk but needs lifelong imaging, and some patients need a further procedure

Calcified atheroma of the aorta and iliac arteries on CT angiography. This is atherosclerotic disease, so a high-intensity statin is recommended and low-dose aspirin is reasonable; he has no history of ulcer or bleeding
Above the 130/80 target, which is recommended for patients with an aneurysm; no blood pressure medicine has been shown to slow aneurysm growth, so the aim is overall cardiovascular risk
No femoral or popliteal aneurysm on examination. A popliteal duplex added to the six-month scan will complete the check, as the examination can miss a small popliteal aneurysm

The options were explained with the figures: continued surveillance now, or repair now, which is not advised at this size; and, at the threshold, endovascular or open repair. He chose surveillance. He said he wants plain numbers at every scan and wants to make each decision himself when the time comes, rather than settling it in advance. He values being able to keep working and walking. If the aneurysm reaches the threshold, he would consider endovascular repair and would want to discuss it again then. He has not chosen to decline repair, and no treatment limits were set

recommendations: Duplex ultrasound every six months while the aneurysm is 5.0 to 5.4 cm, using ultrasound consistently; add a popliteal duplex to the six-month scan
Refer back promptly for repair planning at 5.5 cm, growth of 0.5 cm or more in six months, or any symptom attributable to the aneurysm; endovascular repair is favored on this anatomy
Blood pressure below 130/80; increasing losartan to 100 mg is reasonable, with a metabolic panel afterwards
Continue atorvastatin 40 mg; start aspirin 81 mg daily
Avoid fluoroquinolone antibiotics unless there is no alternative, and anti-inflammatory pain medicines while on aspirin
Emergency plan: call emergency services at once for sudden or severe abdominal, back, flank, or groin pain, fainting, or a tender pulsating lump; carry an aneurysm wallet card
Vascular surgery review at one year, or sooner if a threshold is reached
